questions.question: When would you use map, filter, and reduce in JavaScript?
questions.title: map, filter, and reduce
questions.direct_answer: Use map to transform every array element, filter to keep elements that pass a test, and reduce to combine the array into one accumulated result. These methods return new results rather than changing the source array, although callback code can still mutate referenced objects.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether each array method is connected to its real result shape.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using reduce for every operation or omitting its initial value.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Choosing a loop when control flow makes a method chain less clear.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: map returns one transformed value for each input element.
filter returns only elements whose callback result is truthy.
reduce carries an accumulator and returns one final value.
Provide an explicit initial value to reduce when an empty array is possible.
Use a loop when early exit or several changing states make the chain unclear.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`map`, `filter`, and `reduce` describe three different array operations. `map` preserves the number of elements while transforming each one, `filter` selects a subset, and `reduce` folds the sequence into one result such as a total, lookup object, or grouped structure.

For example, an order page can filter cancelled items, map the remaining items to display rows, and reduce their prices into a total. Each method returns a new array or accumulated value, so the data flow is easier to follow than a loop that performs all three jobs at once.

The callbacks receive the element, index, and original array. Their return values matter: forgetting `return` in a block-bodied callback makes `map` produce `undefined` entries and makes a filter reject everything.

I use these methods when their names match the operation. A plain loop is better when the work needs `break`, `continue`, several accumulators, or one pass whose chained version would allocate unnecessary intermediate arrays.

sections.title: Three verbs, three result shapes
sections.content: Choose the method from the shape of the result: map produces one output per input, filter produces zero or one copy of each input, and reduce produces a single accumulated result.

sections.title: Callbacks do not make nested values immutable
sections.content:
The source array is not structurally changed by these methods, but each element may be an object. Mutating an object inside a callback changes that shared object. A transformation that should preserve earlier state must create new objects deliberately.

Without an initial accumulator, `reduce` uses the first element and begins at the second. That makes an empty array throw a `TypeError` and can produce a different accumulator type than intended. An explicit initial value documents the output type and handles empty input.

sections.title: Operation and result
sections.content:
| Method | Callback answers | Result shape |
|---|---|---|
| `map` | What should this become? | Same length |
| `filter` | Should this stay? | Same or shorter |
| `reduce` | What is the next accumulator? | One final value |

sections.title: Build an order summary

questions.question: When should you use an array instead of an object in JavaScript?
questions.title: Arrays versus objects
questions.direct_answer: Use an array for an ordered sequence that is naturally processed by position or iteration. Use an object for a record with named fields or a simple string-keyed lookup. Arrays are objects internally, but their length and indexed methods give them different application-level meaning.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the collection type follows the meaning of the data.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Recognising when Map offers clearer key semantics.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Arrays represent ordered sequences and use zero-based indexes.
Objects represent records or string/symbol-keyed properties.
Use Array.isArray because typeof an array is object.
Do not use sparse arrays as general-purpose maps.
Use Map when keys are not strings or insertion-order operations dominate.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An array communicates an ordered collection: a list of messages, search results, or steps. It provides indexed access, `length`, iteration, and methods such as `map`, `find`, and `some`.

An ordinary object communicates a record or named lookup. For example, `{ id, name, role }` is clearer as one user record, while an array is appropriate for a sequence of user records. For a dictionary, an object works when keys are known strings and prototype concerns are handled.

Arrays are technically objects, which is why `typeof []` is `"object"`; `Array.isArray` is the reliable test. Giving an array arbitrary string properties does not make those properties part of its indexed length or normal iteration.

The boundary is key behaviour. If keys may be objects, frequent insertion and deletion matter, or exact key types must be preserved, `Map` is often a better lookup. The choice should express the data model rather than merely whichever syntax is shorter.

sections.title: Array and object data-shape choices
sections.content: A record answers “which named fact?” while a sequence answers “which item or position?” Correct modelling gives later code the right methods and prevents accidental dependence on property enumeration.

sections.title: Indexes are special property names
sections.content:
Array indexes are property keys with rules that update `length`. Setting index 5 on an empty array makes its length 6 and leaves holes at earlier positions. Holes behave differently from explicit `undefined` in some array methods, so sparse arrays are rarely a good data structure.

Object property order is specified for modern JavaScript, but relying on an object as if it were a list still hides intent. Convert to an array when ordering, ranking, or repeated traversal is part of the problem.

sections.title: Match the data model
sections.content:
| Need | Better starting shape |
|---|---|
| Ordered list of results | Array |
| One entity with named fields | Object |
| String-keyed lookup | Object or Map |
| Keys of any value type | Map |

questions.question: How do shallow copies of arrays and objects work in JavaScript?
questions.title: Shallow copies and nested references
questions.direct_answer: Spread syntax, Array.from, slice, and Object.assign create a new outer array or object but copy each contained value as-is. Nested objects therefore remain shared references. A true independent copy requires copying the needed nested levels or using a suitable deep-cloning strategy.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether copy syntax is understood beyond surface-level immutability.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Copying only the outer container before mutating a nested object.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connecting structural sharing to reference-based change detection.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Spread creates a new outer array or object.
Nested object references remain shared in a shallow copy.
Mutating a copied top-level primitive field does not affect the source.
Mutating a shared nested object affects both views.
structuredClone handles many data types but not functions or every host object.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A shallow copy creates a new outer container and copies its immediate property values. Primitive property values are copied directly, while an object-valued property contributes the same reference to the copy.

For example, `{ ...profile }` lets the copy receive a different top-level `name` without changing the source, but `copy.address.city = ...` also changes `profile.address.city` unless the address object is copied separately. Array spread follows the same rule for object elements.

This matters in UI state and reducers because a new outer reference can look like an immutable update while a nested object was still mutated. I copy every level along the path that changes, or use a helper whose immutable behaviour is understood.

`structuredClone` is useful for many structured values and circular references, but it throws for functions and cannot preserve every custom behaviour. JSON stringify/parse also loses values such as `undefined` and cannot handle `BigInt` or cycles, so cloning must match the actual data contract.

sections.title: Copy depth is about object boundaries
sections.content: A shallow copy crosses exactly one container boundary. Each nested object creates another boundary that must be copied if the new data needs independent identity at that level.

sections.title: Immutable updates copy the changed path
sections.content:
Suppose application state contains `user.address.city`. Updating only the city requires a new state object, a new user object, and a new address object. Unchanged branches may safely retain their references. This structural sharing is efficient and also lets reference equality identify which branch changed.

A deep copy of an entire object graph is not automatically safer. It can be expensive, can erase prototypes or unsupported values, and can break identity relationships that the program expects. Often the best answer is a focused update of the known schema.

sections.title: Which references change?
sections.content:
source ──► user ──► address
copy   ──► user' ─► address   (shallow: address shared)
copy   ──► user' ─► address'  (nested address copied)
